title: An SNL sketch about caregiving has gone viral. B.C. caregivers explain why
summary: What started as a joke on a late-night sketch comedy show quickly blew up online in the hours following its airing. It’s garnered more than 11.9 million views on Instagram alone, and shared hundreds…

image.caption: Women are still the default caregivers in many family situations, experts say, which is why the SNL sketch has resonated with people around the world. (Photographee.eu/Shutterstock)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

What started as a joke on a late-night sketch comedy show quickly blew up online in the hours following its airing. It’s garnered more than 11.9 million views on Instagram alone, and shared hundreds of thousands of times.
Sister sketch has been seen and shared millions of times since it aired Nov. 14

Comedian John Mulaney stands in the middle of a generic home, his hand on the shoulder of Saturday Night Live cast member Tommy Brennan, who plays his father. Brennan's character can't remember if he took his pills.

"My dad means the world to me, so when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible," Mulaney begins. "I didn't want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aid could cost thousands a week. I didn't know where to turn.
"That's when I heard about Sister," says Mulaney, who describes the service as "a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister."
He goes on to say sisters often take on free, somewhat assumed labour to care for aging parents.
"And I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do," he adds.

The sketch quickly blew up online in the hours after it aired on Nov. 14. It’s garnered more than 12 million views on Instagram alone as of Tuesday afternoon, and shared hundreds of thousands of times.

Barbara MacLean, executive director of Family Caregivers of B.C., says the sketch certainly made the rounds in her office, and while the sketch is funny, there's a deeper message that isn't really funny at all.
Why SNL’s viral 'Sister' sketch hits a nerve with female caregivers in B.C.
It illustrates the ways some family members, often women, are the default caregivers for aging parents, she said.

"You see yourself in that sketch, you laugh, but then you say, 'Wow, this is me,'" MacLean said. "I think there's an awful lot of feeling that's attached to that because it speaks to so many aspects of the caregiving role."
Women carry mental load: MacLean

Carol Dowe, who founded a support group for caregivers on Vancouver Island, said the sketch likely resonated so broadly because baby boomers — of which there are about nine million in Canada, according to the 2021 census — are entering the age where they need care, and their kids are feeling the pressure. Especially women, she added.
"Women tend to be the ones that people turn to in the family," Dowe said.
More and more men are taking on caregiving roles, MacLean said. Statistics Canada data from 2024 suggests nearly half of caregivers are, in fact, men.

blocks.text: However, MacLean said women still carry most of the mental or emotional load of caring for others — not just aging family members. Things like planning ahead, knowing what's in the fridge, keeping track of medical appointments, work commitments, kids' activities — it all piles up, she said.
"Organizing the lives of everybody, the social conveners, the connectors. I think it's natural, you know, caregiving," MacLean said. "It's silent and it's invisible."

She said that while progress has been made, society has a ways to go in terms of equity for women. One way to make a change is to start conversations among family early, so that there's no surprise when mom or dad, or an aunt or uncle, does need assistance, MacLean said.
"That's where we'd love to see society go, and it's going there."
Dowe said caregivers, whether they're men or women, need a break, and she urges families to consider sharing the load.

"They're taking care of their loved one 24/7," Dowe said. "I mean it's everything from weight transfer, going to the bathroom, getting out of bed. And when you're constantly doing this 24 hours around the clock as a caregiver without a break, I mean it takes its toll. And we get edgy as caregivers. We can get angry."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Courtney Dickson is a journalist with CBC News based in Vancouver, covering stories throughout B.C. She has previously worked for CBC in Kamloops and Toronto. She has won Radio Television Digital News Association awards locally and nationally, and in 2022, won a Webster Award.
